genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: an employee lives on the lowest level of the building, next to the front door
his duties fall into three separate categories
the first category covers the cleanliness of the shared areas
he puts a lubricant on the closing mechanisms that make noise
the second category concerns the delivery of letters
he carries the mail to the doors of the oldest residents
the third category consists of calming quarrels between neighbors
he hears the parties to a dispute one after the other
he does not pass on what he learns about the residents' lives
he almost always tracks down the owner of a mislaid object
text: The caretaker of the building lives in a ground-floor unit, right up against the front door. His duties fall into three separate categories. The first is cleaning: he sweeps the stairwell, wipes the glass in the entrance hall, and oils any lock that squeaks. The second is the mail, which he sorts every week and leaves at the doors of the oldest tenants. The third is smoothing over quarrels. When neighbors fall out, he hears each side on its own and then puts forward a settlement both can live with. What earns him his standing, though, is how little he says. He knows the habits of every household and repeats none of it to anyone. Tenants also praise his memory for lost property: a key, a glove, an umbrella left behind in the elevator almost always finds its way back to the owner.

units: the piece of furniture under review was bought secondhand
on arrival its surface was under a sticky coat the seller had not mentioned
that old finish had to be stripped off completely
the supports of the piece began to wobble the following week
simply tightening them cured the fault without taking the whole thing apart
after a season of use the overall verdict is favorable
the material stands up to very hot vessels
one drawer jams when the air turns damp
no adjustment cures that jamming
the piece is judged worth having given how little it cost
text: This low table came secondhand, and the honest verdict on it has come from using the thing. It turned up looking dull, the top under a tacky coat of varnish the seller had said nothing about. Stripping that old finish off completely came first, before there was any hope of a decent result. The following week the legs began to wobble, and tightening them cured it, with no need to pull the whole thing apart. After a season of family use, the verdict leans the right way: the wood shrugs off scalding mugs, scuffs wipe out with a cloth, and the height suits reading as well as a meal taken in front of a screen. One flaw does hold out, though. The drawer jams as soon as the air turns damp, and no adjustment touches it. For what it cost, the table earns its place, so long as you can live with that.

units: the kitchen refit has just been finished
a workman uncovered a cracked pipe behind the washing basin
the seeping had been going on for several weeks
the damp left the wall covering crumbly to the touch
the leak had to be sealed before any finishing work
the water supply had to be shut off during the repair
the dishes were washed at a neighbor's for five evenings
the spending went up and the timings stretched out
the writer invites the person she writes to come and see the room
text: I am writing because the kitchen is finished at last, and you will never guess what held the whole job up. Digging behind the sink, the workman came upon a split pipe. Water had been seeping for weeks, so the plaster crumbled the moment you laid a hand on it. The crack had to be sealed before anyone could think about paint. Since the repair meant shutting off the water, we spent five evenings washing dishes at the neighbor's upstairs. She lent us her basin, and we carried the plates back up the stairs still warm. The upshot: the budget swelled, the timings stretched, and my temper along with them. Now that it has all dried out, the room smells of fresh paint and I sit in there for no reason at all, just to look at the smooth wall. Come and see it for yourself as soon as you can.

units: workshops open to everyone take in household appliances that no longer work
a woman who runs one of these workshops answers what visitors ask
the main obstacle is not that parts are scarce
owners give up because they believe the inside of an appliance is out of reach
the chosen method is to have the visitor carry out the action
the visitor lifts the lid himself and cleans the clogged part
a helper steps in when the repair goes beyond what the visitor can do
this help takes place in front of the owner of the appliance
more objects leave in working order than are left behind
text: What is to be done with a household appliance that has stopped working? The question comes up over and over at repair workshops open to everyone, and the woman who runs one of them answers it readily. The obstacle, she explains, has nothing to do with parts being scarce. Owners give up, sure that a closed casing is out of bounds to them. How do you overturn a belief like that? By having them do the thing instead of describing it: the visitor lifts the lid himself, spots the clogged filter, and scrubs it clean under water. And when the fault runs past what he can manage? A helper takes over, always in front of the person who brought the appliance in, who watches every stage. You measure the outcome in objects that leave in working order, far more of them than are left behind.

units: a resident held that the countryside was better than the noise of an apartment building
her neighbor had lived in both settings
the neighbor disputed that preference
she described the sounds of wood and wind in a house standing on its own
she said that no voice covers those sounds in the countryside
she liked knowing the occupants by their step on the stairs
the first wanted a planted plot and warm water at the outside tap
the second told quiet, which you choose, from company, which you take in
the two women reached no agreement
they greeted each other the next day all the same
text: The tenant below held that the quiet of a country house was worth more than the stir of an apartment building. Her neighbor answered gently that she had known both and believed nothing of the sort. Out there, she said, the wind rubs at the shutters and the floorboards creak with no human voice to cover the sound. You sit and listen to your own solitude. Here, she went on, the stairs ring with steps you know, and each step carries a face: the nurse coming home, the student going out, the child dragging a backpack. The first woman pressed her case all the same. She wanted a garden, the smell of cut grass, water gone warm in the tap outside. The second smiled and said that quiet is chosen, while company is taken in. They parted without agreeing, and greeted each other the next day.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: before running water arrived, three techniques served to wash cloth
the first technique used water mixed with strained ashes
this alkaline solution dissolved greasy matter
the second technique rested on blows struck with a wooden tool
the beaten cloth was then rinsed and left to run off on a hard surface
the third technique spread the cloth out on damp vegetation
damp and radiance together took out the soiling
these methods damaged the fibers, whose weave turned coarse
the wear explains why cloth was counted, mended and handed down
text: Before water arrived under pressure, keeping cloth clean rested on three methods that the old manuals set out in careful detail. The first was an alkaline soak: pieces were stacked in a tub and water strained through ashes was poured over them, and the dissolved potash went to work on grease. The second was mechanical and called for a wooden beater: the fiber was struck against a sloping board, then rinsed under running water and left to drain on a flat stone. The third was sun bleaching. Spread out over wet grass, the cloth gave up its stains to the damp and the light working together. All three wore the material down, and the weave turned coarse to the hand after ten washes or so. That wear is why cloth was counted, mended and handed on from one household to the next like something of value.

units: the observation bears on a kitchen window over one cold night
preparing food gives off steam into the room
this moist air meets a pane that the outside has chilled
the steam turns into droplets settled on the glass
the droplets run together and then travel down the panel
the water gathers against the horizontal piece of wood, which soaks it up
by daybreak the condensation is gone from the glass surface
the wood stays soaked with water in spite of that disappearance
repeating the process lifts the paint and favors fungus
airing the room briefly after cooking halts the process at its start
text: Let us watch what happens at a kitchen window over the course of one cold night. Early in the evening, cooking gives off steam and the room takes on a moisture you cannot see. Toward the end of the meal, that warm air reaches the pane, which the outside has chilled. The steam loses its energy and turns liquid again, and fine drops settle across the glass. Later, drops lying side by side run together, gain weight and slide toward the foot of the frame. They gather against the horizontal rail of wood, which soaks up part of that water. By daybreak the mist has gone from the surface, yet the wood stays soaked through. Repeat that cycle across a whole season and the paint lifts away and fungus gets its opening. Airing the room briefly after cooking halts the chain at its very first link.

units: a bicycle was left against a railing after a change of home
repeated rain attacked the drive, which had seized up
the workshop in the area was quoting a wait of two weeks
so the owner set about the repair with no help
he cleaned every link with a solvent and a stiff brush
the noise of the work drew a neighbor carrying tools
the neighbor trued the back wheel, which had worked loose
that help gave rise to a weekly meeting
the two men repair the objects the building has abandoned
the bin room holds no more hulks
text: The bicycle had been propped against the railing since the end of summer, forgotten after a move. Rain after rain had eaten into the chain, whose links would no longer turn. Because the workshop in the area was quoting a wait of two weeks, the owner decided to set about it alone. He laid the machine on a sheet, poured solvent over the metal, and worked every link with a hard brush. The old grease, gone tacky by then, came away in flakes. The rasp of the bristles drew a neighbor, who came down with an oil can and a open wrench. For want of the right tool, the back wheel had worked loose; the man trued it in a handful of movements. Out of that one favor grew a habit. Once a week the two of them repair whatever the building abandons, and the bin room has emptied of its hulks.

units: a door gives out a shrill noise each time it is moved
the procedure saves calling in a tradesman
you first work out which hinge is at fault by moving the door slowly
a cloth laid underneath protects the floor from runs
you use a thin oil and not a thick paste
a thick paste picks up dirt and makes matters worse
a single drop laid on the pin is enough
moving the door several times spreads the product
you wipe off the excess once it has run down
if the noise carries on, the upper fixing of the hinge has to be tightened
text: So your door shrieks every time it moves, and the noise wakes you up at night? Here is how to be done with it without calling anyone in. Start by working out which hinge is at fault: ease the door open very slowly and listen for where the sound is born. Next, slip a cloth underneath, because what runs off will mark the floor. Take an oil can filled with thin oil, never a thick grease: grease holds dust and the trouble comes back worse. A single drop is enough, laid right on the pin. Swing the door back and forth a dozen times so the liquid works its way down. Let the rest drip out, then wipe the surplus off with the same cloth. If the sound carries on, the top screw has shifted: drive it home, or the door hangs crooked on its hinges. The quiet comes back before the evening is out.

units: two districts side by side have taken opposite approaches to reviving their shops
on the high bank, a sheltered market was built with public money
the pitches there go at a low rent to growers from nearby
attendance at this market reaches its peak at the end of the week
on the lower bank, no building received funding
local people banded together and use an old school yard
each seller sets up a folding stand of his own
the sheltered market draws passing buyers attracted by settled hours
the yard holds a nearby clientele that puts up with bad weather
in both districts, the shops on the streets nearby get more visitors
text: Two districts side by side have taken opposite roads to reviving their local shops, and the contrast leaps straight out at you. On the high bank, a covered market was put up with public money; pitches go at a low rent to growers from nearby, and the crowds peak at the end of the week. On the lower bank, not one building of any kind was funded. Local people banded together into an association and took over an old school yard, where each seller brings a folding stand of his own. The returns differ as much as the settings do. The covered market draws passing buyers, who want shelter and settled hours. The yard holds a nearby following that puts up with rain and improvisation. One point brings the two together: in either district, the shops on the streets nearby have seen more people come through.
